blocks.text: Every football match needs a rulebook that says how many players a side may field, what counts as a foul and who has the final word. A state needs the same thing, only the stakes are higher: who may tax you, who may arrest you, and how they can be removed if they abuse the power. That rulebook is the constitution.

blocks.title: Constitution
blocks.text: The body of agreed rules, written or unwritten, that establishes the organs of government, distributes power among them, defines the relationship between the government and the governed, and sets out the procedure for its own amendment. It is the supreme law of the land: any other law inconsistent with it is void.

blocks.markdown: Section 1(1) of the **Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999** states that the Constitution is supreme and its provisions have binding force on all authorities and persons throughout Nigeria. Section 1(3) adds that if any other law is inconsistent with the Constitution, the Constitution prevails and that other law is void to the extent of the inconsistency. This is what makes a constitution different in kind from an ordinary Act of the National Assembly.

### Sources of a constitution

- **Deliberate enactment** by a constituent assembly or constitutional conference.
- **Statutes and Acts** of the legislature dealing with the machinery of government.
- **Judicial precedents** — decided cases that interpret and settle the meaning of the rules.
- **Conventions and customs** — practices long observed and treated as binding though not written down.
- **Historical documents and charters**, such as Britain's Magna Carta of 1215.
- **Works of eminent authorities** on constitutional law, used to explain and clarify.
- **Colonial and previous constitutions** on which a new document is built.

### Written and unwritten constitutions

A **written constitution** is one whose major provisions are deliberately drafted, codified and assembled in a single formal document. Nigeria, the United States, Ghana and India all have written constitutions.

An **unwritten constitution** is one whose rules are scattered across statutes, judicial decisions, conventions and historical documents rather than gathered into one enactment. Britain is the standard example.

Be careful with the labels. No constitution is entirely written, because conventions always grow up around it, and no constitution is entirely unwritten, since Britain's rules include written statutes such as the Bill of Rights of 1689. The difference is whether the rules have been **codified in one document**.

rows: Clear and precise, so it can be consulted and cited; suitable for federations because it can define the powers of each tier; protects citizens' rights in a form courts can enforce; not easily manipulated by rulers
Rigid and slow to adapt to change; may be too brief to cover new situations; requires interpretation, which puts great power in the hands of judges
Flexible and adapts quickly to changing needs; avoids constitutional crises over technical wording; grows organically out of a people's experience
Vague and uncertain, so it can be twisted; offers weaker protection for minority and individual rights; unsuitable for a federal state; depends heavily on the good faith of rulers
Stable and predictable; guards fundamental rights and the federal bargain against a temporary majority
Difficult to amend even when reform is urgently needed; may frustrate the popular will
Easily amended to meet new circumstances; keeps the law close to public opinion
Open to abuse by a government with a legislative majority; provides little security for rights or for component states
blocks.caption: Merits and demerits of the main types of constitution

blocks.markdown:
### Rigid and flexible constitutions

A **rigid constitution** can only be amended by a special, difficult procedure — a large special majority, the consent of component states, or a referendum. A **flexible constitution** can be amended by the ordinary law-making process, in the same way as any other statute.

Section 9 of the 1999 Constitution makes Nigeria's constitution rigid. An ordinary amendment requires a resolution supported by the votes of **not less than two-thirds of all the members of each House of the National Assembly**, and approval by resolution of the **Houses of Assembly of not less than two-thirds of all the States**. For the most sensitive parts — section 8 (creation of new states and local governments), section 9 itself and Chapter IV on fundamental rights — the bar rises to **four-fifths of all the members of each House**, plus the same two-thirds of state assemblies.

blocks.title: Written does not mean rigid
blocks.text: The two classifications are separate. A constitution is written or unwritten according to whether it is codified in one document; it is rigid or flexible according to how hard it is to amend. Nigeria's is written **and** rigid. Britain's is unwritten **and** flexible. It is possible in principle to be written yet easy to amend, so never treat the pairs as the same distinction.

blocks.markdown:
### Unitary, federal and confederal constitutions

A **unitary constitution** concentrates all sovereign power in one central government, which may delegate functions to local authorities but can also withdraw them. Britain, Ghana and France are examples.

A **federal constitution** divides power between a central government and component state or regional governments, with each deriving its authority from the constitution rather than from the other. Nigeria's 1999 Constitution does this through the Second Schedule, which contains an **Exclusive Legislative List** of 68 items reserved to the National Assembly, and a **Concurrent Legislative List** on which both the National Assembly and the State Houses of Assembly may legislate. Residual matters, not on either list, belong to the states.

A **confederal constitution** leaves sovereignty with the component units, which merely delegate limited powers to a weak central body and retain the right to secede.

Constitutions are also classified as **presidential** or **parliamentary**, according to whether the executive is separate from or drawn out of the legislature.

blocks.title: Classifying the 1999 Constitution of Nigeria
blocks.prompt: Using the classifications in this lesson, describe the 1999 Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria under four headings, giving evidence for each.

steps.text: **Written.** Its provisions were drafted and codified into one formal document of numbered sections and schedules, so it can be cited and consulted. Evidence: the document itself, opened by section 1 declaring its own supremacy.

**Rigid.** Section 9 requires a two-thirds majority of all members of each House of the National Assembly plus approval by two-thirds of the State Houses of Assembly, rising to four-fifths for sections 8 and 9 and for Chapter IV. That is far harder than passing an ordinary Act.

**Federal.** Power is divided between the Federal Government and the 36 states. Evidence: the Exclusive and Concurrent Legislative Lists in the Second Schedule, with residual powers left to the states.

**Presidential.** The President is both Head of State and Head of Government, elected separately from the legislature, and ministers are appointed from outside the National Assembly subject to Senate confirmation.

Add a note of evaluation: because it is written, rigid and federal, the states' powers and citizens' rights cannot be swept away by a simple legislative majority — the chief practical advantage of this combination.

blocks.answer: The 1999 Constitution is written, rigid, federal and presidential — evidenced respectively by its codified text, the amendment procedure in section 9, the legislative lists in the Second Schedule, and the separately elected executive President

blocks.title: Answering "types of constitution" questions
blocks.text: Examiners expect the classifications in pairs: written against unwritten, rigid against flexible, unitary against federal (with confederal added), and presidential against parliamentary. Give one example of each — Nigeria and the United States for written, Britain for unwritten — and never write that Britain has "no constitution". It has one; it is simply not codified.

points: A constitution is the body of rules that creates the organs of government, shares power among them and defines the relationship between government and citizens.
Section 1 of the 1999 Constitution makes it supreme, so any inconsistent law is void to the extent of the inconsistency.
Its sources include deliberate enactment, statutes, judicial precedents, conventions, historical documents, and earlier constitutions.
A written constitution is codified in one document, as in Nigeria and the United States; an unwritten one is scattered across statutes, cases and conventions, as in Britain.
A rigid constitution needs a special procedure to amend it; a flexible one can be amended like any ordinary law.

Section 9 makes Nigeria's constitution rigid, requiring two-thirds of each House of the National Assembly and two-thirds of the State Houses of Assembly, or four-fifths for the most sensitive provisions.
Constitutions are further classified as unitary, federal or confederal, and as presidential or parliamentary.
The 1999 Constitution of Nigeria is written, rigid, federal and presidential.
